abstract: Bangladesh experiences recurrent Nipah virus (NiV) outbreaks and sustained avian influenza virus (AIV) activity. Whether public genomic records contain metadata needed to assess surveillance representativeness across hosts, locations, and time is unclear.We conducted a structured, source-based scoping assessment of publicly documented NiV and AIV genomic records from Bangladesh (2001-2025), drawing on NCBI GenBank/INSDC and cited peer-reviewed and public-health sources. A pilot registry contained 108 entries (55 NiV, 53 AIV). Metadata were retained only when explicitly reported; unverified fields were recorded as not extracted. The registry is not a complete census. Five analytical questions were prespecified; several could not be evaluated because accession-level metadata were unavailable. The 33-accession AIV set containing H5N1 and H3N8 was excluded from H5/H9-specific interpretation. In the pilot registry, 9/108 entries (8.3%) had explicitly reported host species; the separate host-implied category was not added. Twelve entries (11.1%) had a full collection date; 21 (19.4%) had any collection date. Eight entries (7.4%) had an explicit district. The registry lists 22 NiV accession identifiers from a 2026 study, whereas the publication reports 23 newly sequenced N-gene records; this remains unresolved. Eight AIV accessions (PV961349.1-PV961356.1) represent eight segments of one chicken H5N1 isolate, not eight genomes. Twelve MN994-series records are HA-gene sequences from environmental live-bird-market samples.The pilot registry demonstrates substantial metadata limitations. Explicit host information was available for 8.3% of entries and explicit district for 7.4%; these prevent reliable quantitative assessment of host, district-level, and temporal representativeness and do not establish absence of surveillance or viral circulation. Accession-level reconstruction with transparent verification tiers and harmonised identifiers is required before quantitative representativeness indices or district-level priorities can be calculated.
